title: Ellipse and rim
objective: Compare how open a bowl rim looks relative to its width from two eye heights, and draw each observed opening.

warmup.instructions: Keep the bowl fixed and change only your eye height. In seven minutes, sketch its opening from low, middle, and higher positions. Measure each oval's width and height, then order them from flattest to most open.

explanation: A circular, horizontal rim looks flatter as your eye approaches the rim plane. From higher above it, the ellipse opens and more of the inside is visible. The apparent width can also shift, so measure each view separately.
Compare each opening's height with its own measured width. Use that proportion to check the drawing, not as a fixed recipe: let the bowl and your viewpoint set the ellipse.

exercise.instructions:
1. (3 min) Set a bowl on a table and choose a steady horizontal viewing position. Keep the bowl fixed as you change eye height.
2. (6 min) From a low eye height near the rim's level, draw the opening and bowl walls. Measure that rim's apparent width and height.
3. (6 min) Raise your eye. Draw the new opening and side walls; measure this rim's width and height separately.
4. (7 min) Compare the two height-to-width relationships. Note which opening looks flatter and how much more of the inside appears from above.
5. (6 min) Check both bowl contours against life and correct one mismatch in each study if needed.
6. (3 min) Leave the paired views side by side and label the eye heights.

reflection: Which rim is flatter, and how does that relate to your eye height?
How did the measured width and height change between the two views?
What did looking from the second viewpoint make you correct about the bowl?
extension: Try the same comparison with a cup from lesson 08. Notice whether its rim and handle openings flatten by similar amounts.

teaching.whyItMatters: A rim ellipse is a clue to your viewing angle. Comparing two views helps you draw the bowl you see instead of repeating a memorized oval.
teaching.connections: Lesson 8 used the cup's rim to construct a cylinder. Here, revisit that ellipse check with a bowl and add Lesson 4's comparative measurement: compare each opening's height with its own width, then connect the rim to the vessel's side walls.

deepDive: A circular horizontal rim changes its apparent ellipse as your eye moves above or below the rim plane. Near rim height, the opening looks shallow; above the plane, it appears more open and shows more of the inside. Below the plane, the near rim can hide part of the opening. Dodson's ellipse sequence links openness with view angle and illustrates why a drawn oval needs to match the object's position relative to the viewer. This comparison concerns a bowl resting level on a table; tilted vessels and other planes need their own observation.

Measure width and height in each drawing rather than copying the first oval or forcing the two widths to match. If you raise your eye while keeping your horizontal position fixed, you also move farther from the bowl, so its apparent width tends to shrink slightly even as the opening gets taller. Use the ratio as a comparison aid, not a preset target. A center axis can help you check whether both sides balance and reveal pointed ends or a slanted oval. Then connect the rim to the side walls you see, and compare the whole contour with the bowl.

commonMistakes.mistake: Copying one oval into both views or drawing a pointed, tilted rim without checking it.
commonMistakes.lookFor: The two openings stay identical as your eye height changes, or the rim ends pinch and its halves do not balance around the center axis.
